claim: Did you know… smokers are less likely to get Parkinson’s disease?

studies.cite: Mappin-Kasirer et al. (2020), Neurology
studies.finding: In about 30,000 British doctors followed for 65 years, current smokers had 29 percent lower risk of Parkinson disease than never-smokers.
studies.verdict: Dose-related pattern; authors argue it is causal, mechanism unknown.

studies.cite: Domenighetti et al. (2022), Journal of Parkinson's Disease
studies.finding: Mendelian randomisation found genetic liability to smoking initiation inversely associated with Parkinson's disease (odds ratio 0.74).
studies.verdict: Genetic analysis agrees; authors say reverse causation does not explain it.

claim: Did you know… overweight people die less often than people of normal weight?

studies.cite: Flegal et al. (2013), JAMA
studies.finding: Pooled analysis found overweight carried a hazard ratio of 0.94 for all-cause mortality versus normal weight; grade 1 obesity 0.95, not significant.
studies.verdict: The pooled association is real; whether it means protection is disputed.

studies.cite: Banack & Kaufman (2014), Preventive Medicine
studies.finding: In NHANES III, obesity looked protective among people with cardiovascular disease (RR 0.79) but harmful among those without it (RR 1.30).
studies.verdict: Selecting on heart disease can create the effect; authors call it one plausible explanation.

claim: Did you know… low-birth-weight babies of smokers survive better than those of nonsmokers?

studies.cite: Hernández-Díaz, Schisterman & Hernán (2006), American Journal of Epidemiology
studies.finding: In 1991 U.S. data, low-birth-weight infants of smokers had lower infant mortality than those of nonsmokers (relative rate 0.79).
studies.verdict: Artifact of stratifying on birth weight; causal diagrams show no benefit of smoking is needed.

claim: Did you know… hormone therapy protects women from heart disease?

studies.cite: Grodstein et al. (1996), New England Journal of Medicine
studies.finding: In the Nurses' Health Study, women taking estrogen with progestin had a major coronary disease risk ratio of 0.39 versus non-users.
studies.verdict: Observational; not borne out in the later randomized trial.

studies.cite: Writing Group for the Women's Health Initiative Investigators (2002), JAMA
studies.finding: A randomized trial of 16,608 women found 29 percent more coronary events on estrogen plus progestin than placebo; it was stopped early.
studies.verdict: Overturned the heart-protection claim for this regimen and population.

studies.cite: Hernán et al. (2008), Epidemiology
studies.finding: Re-analysing Nurses' Health Study data like a trial, the authors reproduced the trial's early-harm pattern in the intention-to-treat estimates.
studies.verdict: Gap largely traced to time since menopause and follow-up length; debate continues.

claim: Did you know… beta-carotene pills protect smokers from lung cancer?

studies.cite: Alpha-Tocopherol, Beta Carotene Cancer Prevention Study Group (1994), New England Journal of Medicine
studies.finding: In 29,133 Finnish male smokers, those given beta-carotene had 18 percent higher lung cancer incidence and 8 percent higher total mortality.
studies.verdict: Randomized trial: lung cancer went up, not down, in the beta-carotene group.

studies.cite: Omenn et al. (1996), New England Journal of Medicine
studies.finding: Beta carotene plus vitamin A raised lung cancer risk (relative risk 1.28 versus placebo); the trial ended 21 months early.
studies.verdict: Second large trial agreed: no benefit, possible harm.

claim: Did you know… light drinkers outlive people who never drink?

studies.cite: Stockwell et al. (2016), Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs
studies.finding: A meta-analysis of 87 studies found low-volume drinkers had a mortality risk ratio of 0.86 versus lifetime abstainers before adjustment.
studies.verdict: Fell to 0.97 (not significant) once study biases were accounted for.

studies.cite: Millwood et al. (2019), The Lancet
studies.finding: In 512,715 Chinese adults, self-reported drinking showed a U-shaped link to stroke in men, but genotype-predicted intake did not.
studies.verdict: Genetic data suggest the dip is mostly non-causal; the method has its own critics.

claim: Did you know… strangers' prayers helped heart patients leave hospital healthier?

studies.cite: Byrd (1988), Southern Medical Journal
studies.finding: Among 393 coronary care patients, the prayed-for group needed less ventilation, antibiotics and diuretics, and had lower severity scores.
studies.verdict: Many outcome categories tested; length of stay did not differ.

studies.cite: Benson et al. (2006), American Heart Journal
studies.finding: In 1,802 bypass patients, complications were 52 percent with prayer and 51 percent without; patients certain of prayer had 59 percent.
studies.verdict: Larger, better-controlled trial: no benefit from prayer.

claim: Did you know… praying in 2000 shortened hospital stays from the 1990s?

studies.cite: Leibovici (2001), BMJ
studies.finding: For 3,393 bloodstream-infection patients treated 1990 to 1996, prayer in 2000 was linked to shorter stays and fever; mortality did not differ significantly.
studies.verdict: Effect has no plausible mechanism; mortality difference was not significant.

claim: Did you know… placebos work even when patients are told they are placebos?

studies.cite: Kaptchuk et al. (2010), PLoS ONE
studies.finding: In 80 irritable bowel syndrome patients, openly labeled placebo pills beat no treatment on global improvement at 11 and 21 days.
studies.verdict: Small, unblinded, self-reported outcomes.

studies.cite: von Wernsdorff et al. (2021), Scientific Reports
studies.finding: A meta-analysis of 11 trials found a pooled standardized effect of 0.72 for open-label placebos, 0.49 excluding high-risk-of-bias studies.
studies.verdict: Positive, but small trials, self-reported outcomes, funnel-plot asymmetry.

claim: Did you know… transplanting donor feces cures recurrent C. difficile better than antibiotics?

studies.cite: van Nood et al. (2013), New England Journal of Medicine
studies.finding: In 43 patients, duodenal donor-feces infusion cured 15 of 16, versus 4 of 13 on vancomycin and 3 of 13 with lavage.
studies.verdict: Stopped early; FDA approved a fecal microbiota product in 2022.

claim: Did you know… stomach ulcers are caused by bacteria, not stress?

studies.cite: Marshall & Warren (1984), The Lancet
studies.finding: Curved bacilli appeared in gastroscopy biopsies from 58 of 100 patients and were strongly associated with chronic gastritis and ulceration.
studies.verdict: Recognized with the 2005 Nobel Prize; peptic ulcer disease is now considered curable.

claim: Did you know… feeding infants peanuts prevents peanut allergy?

studies.cite: Du Toit et al. (2015), New England Journal of Medicine
studies.finding: In high-risk infants with negative skin tests, peanut allergy at age five was 13.7 percent with avoidance versus 1.9 percent with consumption.
studies.verdict: Randomized trial; the benefit persisted in follow-up.

studies.cite: Du Toit et al. (2016), New England Journal of Medicine
studies.finding: After a further year of peanut avoidance, allergy at age six was 18.6 percent in the avoidance group and 4.8 percent in the consumption group.
studies.verdict: Early introduction protection held up after a year without peanuts.
